abstract: ABSTRACT Next-generation antibodies include a growing number of bispecific and multispecific antibodies that are commonly used to redirect the immune system to fight cancer. Herein, we assessed the depth and breadth of epitope coverage as a proxy for functional diversity in human immune repertoires produced by two complementary in vivo platforms utilizing a common light chain, in a chicken (OmniClic TM ) or rat (OmniFlic®) host species. We adopted NKp46 as a model to target antigen due to its use in emerging natural killer (NK) immune engagers that are being explored clinically as potentially safer alternatives to traditional CD3-based T cell engagers. To probe the epitope diversity of our antibody repertoires, we performed a detailed high throughput epitope binning study using surface plasmon resonance and corroborated our binning assignments with epitope mapping data deduced from hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry. Our results revealed broad epitope coverage and nuanced diversity both within and across repertoires, with few epitopes shared, suggesting that the complementary use of OmniClic TM and OmniFlic® produces more comprehensive coverage than either alone. Furthermore, our epitope binning assignments aligned with our complementarity-determining region-based sequence lineage assignments, enabling a direct comparison of sequence diversity across Clic and Flic repertoires despite their use of different scaffolds, a single functionally rearranged V(D)J scaffold versus multiple combinatorially assembled V(D)J scaffolds, respectively. The rich epitope diversity of both OmniClic TM and OmniFlic® yielded multiple candidates for functional NK activators, as determined in an antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity assay, demonstrating their value as building blocks in constructing optimized immune engagers.

Materials and methods
Trademark acknowledgements

Immunizations and single B cell screening
Immunizations of OmniClic animals with human NKp46 and recovery of B cells were performed as described for OmnidAb animals
34
. The OmniFlic animals were subcutaneously immunized with the same protein antigen in hock every 3–4 days for 6 weeks and B cells were recovered from lymph nodes instead of spleen. Single B cells were screened on the xPloration instrument, a microcapillary-based array screening system
33
using a bead-adsorbed protein target or a stable NKp46 CHO cell line (CHOK1-NKp46-Cell-Line, Kyinno Biotechnology, catalog number KC-1789). Hits were sequenced and unique-sequence clones were synthesized from custom-ordered DNA, expressed as full-length IgG1 and protein-A purified, prior to analytical characterization.
NGS processing
NGS data is preprocessed using pRESTO (0.7.1) from the Immcantation (Version 4.4.0) package and the resulting reliable antibody sequences from the preprocessing are annotated using IgBlast (1.18.0) that sources custom libraries for our OmniFlic- and OmniClic-derived antibodies. We then performed lineage analysis, clustering sequences with the same V and J gene, same heavy-chain CDR3 length, and an edit distance of two amino acids in the heavy-chain CDR3 region, to the annotated sequences from NGS libraries. When selecting clones, we first narrowed down to the lineages that contain both bead binders and cell binders from high throughput screening technique xPloration, reasoning that there is statistically high confidence in those lineages to bind with the target of interest. Clones are further selected using two methods. Method A selects clones based on the clone representation, picking the top and bottom 10 greatest representation clones from each overlap lineage. Method B selects clones that span across most lineages to capitalize on the diversity of the sequence space; the number of selected clones within each lineage is proportional to the size of the lineage. After selecting clones from both methods, we apply the liability assessment on both sequence and structural level to eliminate clones that have a high-risk developability issue.
Hit expansion
The data used for model building and selection included 69,000 unique heavy-chain amino acid sequences from NGS on three different OmniClic common light-chain chickens immunized with NKp46. Sequences were filtered for duplicate count greater than or equal to two. Activity data was provided for 178 unique amino acid sequences. Of the 178 sequences with activity data, 90 were inactive and the remaining 88 sequences had K
D
values ranging from 2 to 500 nM. Error values for the 88 active sequences were obtained by propagating uncertainty for association and dissociation kinetic rate constants (k
a
and k
d
) from the SPR measurements. K
D
values were scaled by -log2(K
D
) with inactive values set to zero corresponding to a K
D
2000 nM. This placed all the activity data for regression in the range of 0 to 10.
Variational autoencoder model
Antibody sequences were modeled using a VAE model
49
,
50
. Input sequences were embedded using 1-hot encoding into a 21 × 134 matrix where 21 corresponds to the 20 standard amino acids plus an end character and 134 is the maximum sequence length. Encoding was performed using an LSTM layer with 134 nodes and dropout regularization followed by batch normalization. The size of the latent layer was 50 nodes and was modeled using a multivariate normal distribution from tensorflow-probability with learned variances and covariances. The prior was a N(0,1) distribution and KL weight was 0.75. The decoder layer consists of an upsampling dense layer of size 67 × 36 followed by a 1D deconvolutional layer with 18 filters and kernel size and strides of 2 and ReLU activation, and an LSTM layer with 134 nodes. Each of the preceding 3 layers in the decoder is followed by batch normalization. A final dense layer of 21 nodes
50
forms the model output. A Gaussian progress regression model also comes off the latent layer. This model has one dense variational layer with trainable prior and 1 node with ReLU activation followed by a Gaussian Process regression layer. Dropout regularization is applied off of the latent layer input to the regression layer. Overall, the Encoder has ~260K trainable parameters, the decoder has ~210K trainable parameters and the regression model has 230 trainable parameters for a total of ~470K trainable parameters.
Model training
Model training was performed for 500 epochs using a batch size of 500 using an Adam optimizer with Nesterov momentum with a learning rate of 0.002. The autoencoder and Gaussian progress regression models were trained simultaneously in one global model. Loss weights of 1 and 50 were applied to the reconstruction loss and Gaussian process log-likelihood loss, respectively.
Clone selection
Sequences were selected from the VAE model using the Expected Improvement (EI) Bayesian Optimization acquisition function. All sequences with an EI value greater than an internal reference set by sequences with a measured affinity <25 nM. Sequences were filtered for liabilities at the structural level. In this case, six homology models were generated per sequence using the Molecular Operating Environment (MOE) software. Mean and standard deviation of the standard descriptors used in MOE were computed across all six models and these values were used for filtering the selection.
Surface plasmon resonance
Binding kinetics (capture kinetics) and epitope binning (classical sandwich) experiments were conducted using a high-throughput SPR (HT-SPR) on Carterra’s LSA platform equipped with HC30M as previously described
34
. Recombinant His-tagged human NKp46 protein was produced in-house (Uniprot Accession # O76036-1, residues 22 to 255) or sourced from Acro Biosystems (cat. no. NC1-H52H4) and recombinant His-tagged cyno NKp46 protein was sourced from Acro Biosystems (cat. no. NC1-C52H4). NKp46 proteins were polished by preparative size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) and monomeric fractions were isolated immediately prior to use. An anti-His mAb was used as a universal sandwiching control for all epitope binning experiments. Data were processed, analyzed, and figures generated using the Carterra EP™ software. Clones that performed as both ligand and analyte were amenable to a fully comprehensive bidirectional analysis, whereas clones that failed as ligand, were tested as analyte-only and therefore were not tested for mutual competition. To simulate a full heat map to facilitate hierarchical clustering into epitope communities, the blocking data from the 119 × 33 ‘many-on-few’ analyte-on-ligand heat map was used to infer ‘missing’ data (for analyte-only clones lacking a ligand counterpart) by transposing the measured blocking results (block or not block) and assuming a fully symmetrical pairwise competition matrix. The ‘inferred’ reconstructed heat map was then subjected to a user-defined cut-height to generate 14 epitope ‘communities’ (S3 Fig).
HDX-MS epitope mapping
Samples for HDX-MS analysis were named as follows: Sample-7 (F31), Sample-8 (F23), Sample-10 (C24), Sample-11 (C08), Sample-12 (C70), Sample-13 (C65), and Sample-15 (D01). Sample-7 to Sample-12 were analyzed in a separate experiment than Sample-13 and Sample-15. In-house-produced NKp46 was used for the HDX-MS experiments.
Sample preparation
HDX reactions comparing apo NKp46 to NKp46 incubated with Sample-7 to Sample-12 were carried out in a 10 µl reaction volume containing 30 pmol of NKp46 and 30 pmol of Sample-7 to Sample-12. The exchange reactions were initiated by the addition of 7.8 µL of D2O buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 92.6% D2O (V/V)) to 2.2 µL of protein (final D2O concentration of 72.3%). HDX reactions comparing apo NKp46 to NKp46 incubated with Sample-13 and Sample-15 were carried out in a 15 µl reaction volume containing 30 pmol of NKp46 and 30 pmol of Sample-13 or Sample-15. The exchange reactions were initiated by the addition of 11.8 µL of D2O buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 92.6% D2O (V/V)) to 3.2 µL of protein (final D2O concentration of 72.8%). Reactions proceeded for 10s, 100s, 1000s and 10000s at 20°C before being quenched with ice cold acidic quench buffer, resulting in a final concentration of 0.6 M guanidine HCl and 0.9% formic acid post quench. All conditions and timepoints were created and run in independent triplicate. Samples were flash frozen immediately after quenching and stored at −80°C until injected onto the ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) system for proteolytic cleavage, peptide separation, and injection onto a QTOF or Orbitrap for mass analysis, described below.
Protein digestion and MS/MS data collection
Protein samples were rapidly thawed and injected onto an integrated fluidics system containing a HDx-3 PAL liquid handling robot and climate-controlled (2°C) chromatography system (LEAP Technologies), a Waters Acquity UPLC I-Class Series System, as well an Orbitrap Exploris 120 Mass Spectrometer (ThermoFisher). The full details of the automated LC system were previously described
51
. The samples were run over an immobilized pepsin column (Affipro; AP-PC-001) at 200 µL/min for 4 minutes at 2°C. The resulting peptides were collected and desalted on a C18 trap column (Acquity UPLC BEH C18 1.7 µm column (2.1 × 5 mm); Waters 186,004,629). The trap was subsequently eluted in line with an ACQUITY 300Å, 1.7 μm particle, 100 × 2.1 mm BEH C18 UPLC column (Waters), using a gradient of 3–10% B (Buffer A 0.1% formic acid; Buffer B 100% acetonitrile) over 1.5 minutes, followed by a gradient of 10–25% B over 4.5 minutes, followed by a gradient of 25–35% B over 5 minutes, finally, after 1 minute, at 35% B a gradient of 35–80% B over 1 minute was used. MS experiments acquired over a mass range from 150 to 2200 m/z using an electrospray ionization source operated at a temperature of 200°C and a spray voltage of 4.5 kV. Same LC system, gradient and columns were used for all samples.
Peptide identification
Peptides were identified from the non-deuterated samples of NKp46 using data-dependent acquisition following tandem MS/MS experiments (precursor scan from 300 to 1500 m/z, 4 data dependent scans from 300 to 1500 m/z, dynamic exclusion set to
n
= 1 with 10s exclusion time, 6s expected LC peak width on Orbitrap system). MS/MS datasets were analyzed using FragPipe v18.0 and peptide identification was carried out by using a false discovery-based approach using a database of purified proteins and known contaminants
52–54
. MSFragger was utilized, and the precursor mass tolerance error was set to −20 to 20 ppm. The fragment mass tolerance was set at 20ppm. Protein digestion was set as nonspecific, searching between lengths of 4 and 50 aa, with a mass range of 400 to 5000 Da.
Mass analysis of peptide centroids and measurement of deuterium incorporation
HD-Examiner Software (Sierra Analytics) was used to automatically calculate the level of deuterium incorporation into each peptide. All peptides were manually inspected for, for example, correct charge state, correct retention time, and appropriate selection of isotopic distribution. Deuteration levels were calculated using the centroid of the experimental isotope clusters. Results are presented as relative levels of deuterium incorporation and the only control for back exchange was the level of deuterium present in the buffer (72.3% or 72.8%). Differences in exchange in a peptide were considered significant if they met all three of the following criteria: ≥5% change in exchange, ≥0.4 Da difference in exchange, and a
p
value <0.01 using a two-tailed student T-test. Samples were only compared within a single experiment and were never compared to experiments completed at a different time with a different final D2O level. The data analysis statistics for all HDX-MS experiments are in S3 Table according to published guidelines
55
(see S1 File for the source data file). The MS proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository
56
with the dataset identifier (PXD069455).
In-vitro developability assessment of anti-NKp46 antibodies
Thermal stability (Tm) and aggregation (Tagg) were determined by differential scanning fluorimetry (UNCLE-0330, Unchained Labs); and homogeneity and purity were assessed by analytical SEC as described previously
34
.
Generation of antibody models and in silico assessment of potential liabilities and post-translational modifications
For each of the eight clone sequences of interest (F15, F23, F31, C08, C24, C44, C65, C70), 25 Fv models were generated using Antibody modeler in MOE
57
. In all cases, a maximum of five different frameworks and five different CDR combinations of structural templates were used. All models generated were then subjected to energy minimization prior to structure-based annotation of potential post-translational modifications and liabilities. Liability score A, derived from previous work by Thorsteinson et al.
58
, was calculated for each model. It reflects the presence of exposed high-risk Asn deamidation and Asp isomerization motifs in the CDRs or framework, potential glycosylation sites within the CDRs, total CDR length, Fc total charge, VH-VL absolute charge difference, and size of CDR hydrophobic patch areas. We also used these models to evaluate potential unpaired cysteines in the CDRs and aggregation prone motifs (none to be reported), as well as to calculate the average isoelectric point (pI) and net charge at neutral pH
57
.
Production of bispecific antibodies for ADCC
Clones C08, C44, and F15 were selected for reformatting into a symmetrical tetravalent 2 + 2 scFv-IgG Morrison format using cetuximab scFv tethered from the C-terminal of the heavy chain (HC) or light chain (LC) of NKp46 Clic or Flic IgG backbone. Constructs were prepared in pairs: one construct had an active IgG1-Fc, the other incorporated STR silencing mutations
59
. Plasmids were constructed by following the manufacturer’s protocol of Gibson Assembly® Cloning Kit (NEB, E5510S) and amplified with EndoFree Plasmid Maxi Kit (Qiagen, 12,362). Proteins were expressed in HEK293 cells and protein-A purified followed by preparative SEC (Fig. S5c and S5d).
Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity assay
A 2D ADCC assay was performed by Charles River Laboratories, Inc. using the IncuCyte Live-Cell Analysis System for continuous visualization and automated analysis of immune cell-mediated killing of tumor cells (Sartorius, Inc). Donor-derived NK cells and EGFR-expressing target cells (A549) were used to test a panel of eight NKp46 X EGFR bispecific compounds, representing two Morrison formats. Six total donors were used, split into cohorts of three donors per Morrison format (to test four compounds per set of three donors) and each experimental condition was tested in triplicate. Each immune-assay readout was performed once. Readouts were tumor cell growth over time by IncuCyte.
The ADCC assay comprised 4 steps: target cell seeding, CD56-positive cells isolation, tumor killing assay, and data analysis, as follows. NucLight Red (NLR) expressing A549 cells were cultured under standard aseptic conditions. On day −1 these cells were seeded into Poly-L-Lysine coated 96-well plates at 7.5x10
3
cells/well. Human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from three healthy donors via density gradient separation. CD56+ NK cells were isolated from PBMCs by magnetic separation and CD56 purity was confirmed by flow cytometry prior to co-culture with target A549 tumor cells. Following CD56+ cell isolation, NK cells were incubated with target tumor cells expressing the NucLight Red (NLR) nuclear dye at a 10:1 effector:target (E:T) ratio. Co-cultures were incubated with 20 µg/mL bispecific compounds. Appropriate controls were included: tumor cells alone, tumor cells/NKs in the presence of 20 µg/ml Cetuximab (IgG1 targeting EGFR Control), 20 µg/ml IgG1 isotype control, 1 µM bortezomib (cytotoxic control) or 10 ng/ml IL-2+IL-12+IL-15 (NK activation positive control). Tumor cell growth was determined as the total red count (A549 NLR cells) per well normalized to
T
= 0. Area under curve (AUC) growth data was calculated in GraphPad Prism and reported as mean ± SEM (shown as error bars) of triplicate biological replicates. All samples were compared with untreated or vehicle (PBS alone): see S2 File for statistical T-tests.

body:
Introduction
Therapeutic antibodies have revolutionized medical treatment options for patients, especially those suffering from cancer and autoimmune disorders
1–3
. Compared with other drug modalities, antibodies offer advantages of exquisite specificity, high affinity, and long serum half-life, minimizing the dose and frequency of dosing needed to produce a safe and efficacious response in patients
4
. Antibodies can be used in various ways to bring therapeutic benefit to patients, and this is reflected in the myriad of molecular formats in approved and clinical-stage drugs, as driven by the intended biological mechanism of action
5
.
The molecular and functional diversity of antibodies is further expanded by the increasing number of bispecifics that have been approved in recent years
6–8
fueled by a robust clinical pipeline with emerging multi-specifics
9–12
. A major mechanism of action for approved bispecifics is immune cell engagement, a type of immunotherapy where the antibody helps the body to fight cancer
13
,
14
. In this type of bispecific antibody, one specificity recruits an immune cell, typically a T cell via the CD3 receptor on its surface, and the other redirects it to a tumor cell, via tumor-associated receptors such as EpCAM, CD19, CD20, BCMA, GPRC5D, or DLL3, thereby mobilizing immune cells directly to the tumor site where they activate immune cell-mediated anti-tumor immune responses, while sparing healthy cells.
Most approved anti-CD3 bispecifics are used to treat blood cancers such as lymphoma, myeloma, and leukemia, with limited success achieved in treating solid tumors
15–17
. As a drug class, use of CD3-directed bispecifics is often hampered by significant dose-limiting toxicities, especially cytokine release syndrome
18
. The design of CD3 engagers continues to evolve to overcome these challenges by optimizing the antibody’s binding affinity, valency, epitope specificity including logic gating and targeting specific T cell subsets, conditional activation, and molecular geometry, among other considerations
19
. As an alternative to T cell engagers, next-generation clinical-stage immune engagers are also exploring the use of other types of immune cells such as natural killer (NK) cells
20
that can be targeted via activating receptors such as CD16a and NKp46
21
,
22
.
Since ‘one size does not fit all’ when optimizing the molecular format of a bispecific and multi-specific antibodies
10
, technologies that facilitate the combination of disparate variable antibody domains as building blocks for custom molecular constructs are appealing. Within the engineering toolbox used to assemble biotherapeutics are common light chain (cmLC) antibodies
23
, an elegant approach that eliminates the light-chain mispairing problem of traditional IgG-like bispecifics and facilitates their manufacture
24
without compromising target-binding affinity
25
. The blockbuster drug emicizumab (Hemlibra®), which represents the first cmLC bispecific antibody to be approved by the Food and Drug Administration (in 2017), has transformed the treatment options for the clinical management of hemophilia A
26
. Several cmLC antibodies are in clinical development
27
,
28
. An under-appreciated but substantial practical convenience of cmLC antibodies is in the screening stages of a de novo discovery campaign because they obviate the need to preserve native heavy and light-chain pairing, and thereby reduce selections to just the native heavy chain variable domain, which has been optimized to pair with a germline cmLC.
We set out to explore the binding kinetics, affinity, epitope diversity, developability, and biological functional activity of antibodies from the immunization of OmniClic
TM
(abbreviated as ‘Clic’) animals, a cmLC platform producing fully human-sequence immune repertoires in a chicken host, which is a divergent, single-scaffold gene-converting species
29
. We benchmarked our results against immunization of OmniFlic® (abbreviated as ‘Flic’) animals, a cmLC platform that produces fully human-sequence immune repertoires in a rat host species and is an established industry standard used in clinical-stage CD3-bispecifics: etentamig (CD3 X BCMA)
30
and surovatamig (CD3 X CD19)
31
. As a model target, we chose NKp46, an activating receptor on NK cells that has gained popularity in clinical-stage multi-specific immune engagers
21
,
32
. We posit that NKp46 antibodies from our immune repertoires showing functional activation could be reformatted as bispecific or multispecifics to provide versatile options for constructing next-generation immune engagers.
Results
OmniClic and OmniFlic repertoires produce comparably diverse kinetics and affinities
NKp46-specific antibodies generated from protein immunizations of Clic and Flic animals were isolated in a single B cell workflow using the xPloration® instrument, a microcapillary-based array screening system
33
, and tested for their target-binding kinetics and affinities by surface plasmon resonance (SPR). Initial phenotypic selections yielded a similar number of unique-sequence clones from each repertoire (44 Flic and 45 Clic) with diverse-binding kinetics and affinities spanning a similar range, with K
D
values from 0.5 nM to 200 nM, with many showing K
D
values comparable to the benchmarks, which were single-digit nM (
Figure 1a,b
, and S1 Fig).
Figure 1.
Binding kinetics and affinities for human NKp46. (A) Isoaffinity plot and (B) Scatter plot for human NKp46 affinity determinations of Clic (AI-expanded hits; original with or without ‘seeds,’ which are clones selected for AI hit-expansion based on their high-affinities), Flic, and benchmarks (see S1 table). (C) Scatter plot of binding affinities for human NKp46 compared with cyno NKp46 for a subset of clones (see S2 table). In panel C, Clic clones from original, seed, and AI-hit expansion are treated as one ‘repertoire.’ Data in panels A and B were determined using in-house-produced NKp46, whereas data in panel C was determined using commercially sourced (Acro) proteins.
Variational autoencoder-based hit expansion retrieved higher affinities than those from phenotypic selections
To retrieve even higher affinity clones than those from our phenotypic selections, we performed a data-driven antibody hit expansion of Clic repertoires using a variational autoencoder (VAE) trained on next-generation sequencing (NGS) data from the same immunized antibody repertoires. Artificial intelligence (AI)-expanded hits were, on average, 10-fold higher affinity than those from our original phenotypic selections. This improvement can be seen in the iso-affinity plot and K
D
scatter plot shown in
Figures 1a,b
, respectively, where AI-expanded hits (in red) ‘burst’ from the ‘seeds’ (in cyan) giving slower dissociation rate constants, resulting in lower K
D
values. Additionally, we selected a subset of clones for binding affinity to cynomolgus (cyno) NKp46 (sharing 86% identity with human NKp46) and found many cyno cross-reactive clones within both Clic and Flic repertoires. We also found examples of human-specific NKp46 clones that did not cross with cyno NKp46 (see S2 Table).
Clic and Flic repertoires show broad and complementary epitope coverage
We performed a detailed and statistically powered high-throughput (HT) epitope binning study on a merged panel of clones from Clic and Flic repertoires to assess the breadth and depth of their epitope coverage. We incorporated a small panel of literature clones (Innate-1, 2, 3, 4, and 9)
32
as benchmarks to determine whether our antibodies could overlap known epitopes and expand coverage beyond them. Of these five benchmarks, two (Innate-1 and Innate-4) served as structural benchmarks (PDB:6IAP). Innate-1, 2, 3, and 4 reportedly target distinct, non-overlapping epitopes, which we empirically confirmed (S2 Fig). Innate-2 and Innate-9 reportedly overlap with one another. We also included three previously described single domain heavy chain-only antibodies (OmnidAb® clones, herein called ‘dAbs’) as tool compounds defining the Innate-3 epitope
34
.
Figure 2
shows network plots from an epitope binning analysis of 119 total clones comprising 70 Clic (including expanded hits), 41 Flic, five benchmarks, and three dAbs. In a network plot, each node is a unique antibody and each chord connecting two nodes suggests a blocking relationship between the two antibodies. It is assumed that all antibodies have been tested against one another in a combinatorial pairwise manner such that the absence of a connecting chord between two nodes indicates the lack of a blocking relationship, which is detected in our so-called “classical sandwich” epitope binning assay format, as the formation of a ternary or “sandwich” complex, due to the binding of a solution antibody (as analyte) to NKp46 that is first tethered by an immobilized antibody (as ligand) on our SPR chip surface. Based on the observed (or in some cases, inferred) blocking relationships (see Methods), antibodies are clustered into epitope groups. To determine an appropriate clustering level, we first assigned clones to five groups or ‘super-communities’ and named them (1 through 5) based on their blocking relationships with the benchmarks (Innate-1, 2, 3, 4 and none); these were then split into more granular groupings to give a total of 14 ‘communities,’ as shown by the network plot in
Figure 2a
that is colored by community.
Figure 2.

Despite their non-overlapping epitopes, Innate-1 and Innate-4 epitopes were strongly overlapped by a large group of clones, likely due to immunogenicity of those epitopes and our Clic AI hit-expansion that focused on four communities (1, 4a, 4b, and 4C1). Three Flic clones fall into the Innate-3 community (Com-3), anchored by our Innate-3-like dAb clones. We identified a Special epitope cluster distinct from and non-overlapping with the benchmark comprising Flic (Com-Sf) and Clic (Com-Sc) clones. Another novel epitope cluster connecting Innate-1 and Innate-2 is composed Com-1C2a and Com-1C2b. Of the 14 defined communities, six were Clic-only and six were Flic-only with two shared across Clic and Flic (
Table 1
). As observed in
Figure 2b
, where the nodes are colored by repertoire, Flic recapitulated the epitopes of all benchmarks tested, while Clic only recapitulated that of Innate-2 (which fell into the same community as Innate-9). Taken together, Clic and Flic produced clones that blocked the benchmarks in many ways as seen by the complex network of chords emanating from the benchmarks connecting Clic and Flic clones that cross-talked across communities. Additionally, Clic and Flic accessed epitopes not represented by the benchmarks, as shown by nodes that have no chords (no blocking relationships) connecting them to any benchmarks.

Detailed epitope binning studies reveal nuanced epitope diversity that is corroborated by epitope mapping
To justify the community-level grouping of our SPR-based high throughput binning approach, hydrogen deuterium eXchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) was used to epitope-map a subset of clones. HDX-MS measures the exchange rate of amide hydrogens, with this rate primarily dependent on secondary structure stability, making it well suited to capturing changes conformational dynamics induced by antibody–antigen interactions
35
,
36
. Differences in deuterium exchange were deemed significant if they fulfill all the following criteria: percent difference greater than 5%, difference in number of deuterons incorporated greater than 0.4 and p-value less than 0.01 after applying a two-tailed T-Test (n = 3). The peptide coverage of NKp46 was ~40%, with any epitopes present in these regions being unmappable. This is not uncommon in heavily disulfide-linked proteins
37
. Despite these challenges, we were able to define conformational differences in NKp46 upon binding to distinct classes of antibodies. When interpreting HDX-MS results, understanding that differences can be caused by direct-binding interactions (epitopes), but also by allosteric conformational changes, is critical. To explore epitope breadth, we chose clones from distinct epitope communities (1C2b, 2a, 2 U, 3, and 4C1) and, to explore epitope depth, we chose clones from the same community (2a) showing highly similar blocking profiles. The alignment across our binning and HDX-MS mapping studies reinforced the reliability of our binning experiments (
Table 2
).

Both Clic and Flic repertoires yielded functional NK engagers across various epitope communities
We next investigated whether our NKp46 antibodies could induce NK cell-mediated killing of tumor cells in an antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) assay. To enable the use of a well-established EGFR-expressing cancer cell line (A549) we formatted our NKp46 antibodies as EGFR bispecifics using a symmetrical tetravalent 2 + 2 scFv-IgG Morrison format
38
, a commonly used format for producing multispecifics and among the many used in clinical-stage NK engagers
12
,
39
and in preclinical studies
40
. We tethered cetuximab scFv from an anti-NKp46 IgG backbone, explored two different tethering locations (at C-terminal of the heavy chain or light chain) and tested both STR-silenced (mAbsolve, see Methods for details) and active IgG1-Fc backbones to determine whether NKp46-engagement alone was sufficient to produce ADCC (on a silent Fc backbone), and whether NKp46 engagement could augment ADCC on an active Fc backbone (via the ‘normal’ CD16a/IgG1-Fc-mediated activation). Three clones from disparate epitope communities with similar or higher affinities than the benchmarks were selected for reformatting into EGFR bispecifics. From Clic, we chose C08 because of its unique epitope (Com 2 U) and C44 (Com 4C1) because of its high affinity and tested each of them in a different Morrison format. From Flic, we chose F15 (Com 4a) and tested it in both Morrison formats.
We first confirmed that the bispecific compounds had negligible effect on the growth of tumor target cells alone in the absence of NK cells along with appropriate controls (S5 Fig). Discussion
Clic’s single germline scaffold facilitated AI hit expansion
Clic’s use of a single germline scaffold facilitated our AI-assisted hit expansion and successfully retrieved clones with an order of magnitude higher affinity than the ‘seeds,’ representing high-affinity clones from original selections. The VAE approach is agnostic to prior structural or functional knowledge of antibodies, relying solely on the observed sequence and activity data. This enables unbiased exploration of the sequence landscape and supports the discovery of diverse, functionally relevant antibody candidates beyond known motifs or germline constraints. Unlike rodents and most mammals, including humans, that use V(D)J (variable-diversity-joining) recombination as a primary mechanism to diversify their repertoires from the combinatorial assembly of multiple gene segments, the chicken is a single-scaffold species relying instead on gene conversion, starting with a functionally rearranged V(D)J gene
41
. Clic, an engineered chicken, leverages the chicken host’s natural mechanisms of diversification. Our lineage definition allowed direct comparison of epitope diversity across Clic and Flic repertoires despite them reaching diversity in different ways: single scaffold versus multiple, combinatorially assembled scaffolds.
High throughput epitope binning uncovered nuanced and complementary diversity
Herein, we demonstrate that Clic and Flic repertoires provide complementary platforms for producing
in vivo
-optimized human immune repertoires for drug discovery, yielding high-affinity clones with cyno cross-reactivity, broad epitope coverage, and functional activity as NK engagers. In addition, our clones exhibited favorable developability properties when assessed by both
in-silico
and
in-vitro
methods (S5 Table). Our detailed epitope binning study revealed that both repertoires showed broad and complementary coverage, with most epitope communities being found in only one repertoire and not another, and few shared epitope communities. This intricate diversity can be appreciated in the community network plot (
Figure 2b
), the Venn diagram (
Figure 4d
) and
Table 1
, which collectively show the distribution of epitope communities within and across repertoires. We intersected our analysis with a small panel of literature benchmarks sourced from the immunization of mouse
32
. Flic was able to recapitulate their epitopes when analyzed at the epitope community level in our analysis. While Clic only recapitulated one of them (the Innate-2/9 epitope), Clic generated many Clic-unique epitope communities. This additional epitope coverage may reflect Clic’s different recognition of human targets relative to mammalian host species (rodents) because the chicken is a divergent host species
42
. Both Clic and Flic expanded epitope coverage beyond the benchmarks and provided multiple cyno cross-reactive clones from different epitope communities (
Figure 1c
and S2 Table).
It is well-established that high throughput epitope binning assay can discriminate antibodies, aiding in the triage of large antibody panels to prioritize candidates for further study
43–45
and that the deduced epitope differences can be confirmed by structural methods
46–48
, increasing confidence in binning assignments that may allow for the identification of antibodies with differentiated binding modes and unique mechanisms of actions. However, to fully appreciate the depth and breadth of epitope coverage contained in antibody repertoires, a few caveats must be met to optimize the information content of these assays. Not only are the choice and number of antibodies used for probing epitope coverage key but the ‘granularity’ of binning assignments is often a subjective exercise, relying on both good biosensor practices and statistically powered experimentation.
In Gauthier et al.’s assessment of 17 NKp46 clones, the authors observed that NKp46-2 (Innate-2) and NKp46-9 (Innate-9) cross-block one another but are non-identical because they can be differentiated by other antibodies (NKp46-8 and NKp46-12)
32
(see S2 Fig). While our study recapitulated their observation that Innate-1, 2/9, 3, and 4 target non-overlapping epitopes, we were unable to distinguish between Innate-2 (B02) and Innate-09 (B09) because we lacked such a discriminatory antibody, despite analyzing a much larger panel of (119) antibodies. This shows that, while increasing the number of antibodies in an epitope binning study increases the chances of finding antibodies that resolve epitope differences between highly similar epitopes, a smaller panel can suffice if they contain appropriate discriminatory power.
While we attempted an empirical full 119 × 119 pairwise competition of our multi-repertoire merged panel of clones, most clones (73%) did not regenerate as ligand when tested in a classical sandwich assay format. Despite significant ligand attrition, we were still able to assign epitope communities to all antibodies in the study by relying on a core set of antibodies that performed well bidirectionally (as both analyte and ligand) and using them as ligands to probe a larger set of analyte-only tested clones. Our approach yielded precise epitope discrimination that was corroborated by epitope mapping data using HDX-MS, and our community assignments matched the granularity of sequence lineage assignments, further validating our approach. Com-4C1 mapped to residues
L39-F62
, Com-3 mapped to
H108-F121
, and Com-2a (all three members tested) was anchored by residues
L135-Y147
(
Table 2
).
Molecular format affects the potency of NK engagers
Our ADCC results showed that NKp46 antibodies from Clic and Flic targeting different epitopes could all reduce tumor cell growth to varying extents on a silent-Fc backbone, via a mechanism independent of the CD16a-mediated pathway. Format mattered, as LC-tethered scFv-IgGs appeared more potent than HC-tethered scFv-IgGs. Affinity did not seem to drive potency as C44, our highest affinity clone (with K
D
value of 70 pM) was not the most potent, although it was only tested as an LC-tethered scFv-IgG, suggesting its potency may be improved if tested in an alternate, more optimum, format. Silenced Fc bispecifics could outperform their active Fc counterpart, suggesting that the molecular geometry could be optimized to favor co-engagement of both NK activation pathways (NKp46-mediated and CD16a/active-Fc-mediated). Indeed, molecular format, size, geometry, and valency are important factors that must be co-optimized in designing therapeutic NK engagers
12
,
39
.
While the cmLC technology is conventionally used to simplify the generation of a 1 + 1 IgG-like format using a knobs-into-holes or similar Fc heterodimerization strategy, this study leveraged cmLC antibodies in an alternative configuration to create multivalent NK engagers. This approach was selected because multivalent formats are widely regarded as optimal for NK engagement, as supported by both literature and clinical evidence. Specifically, we utilized cmLC NKp46 antibodies to construct Morrison formats in which a benchmark anti-EGFR antibody (cetuximab) was incorporated as an scFv at various positions within a cmLC anti-NKp46 IgG backbone.
Notably, use of cmLC in a 1:1 IgG-like format necessitates that both target specificities (NKp46 and EGFR) be generated using the same cmLC platform. However, as this study focused exclusively on the discovery of novel NKp46 clones without a concurrent campaign against a tumor-associated target, we adopted an alternative strategy. We leveraged established ADCC assays using a commonly utilized EGFR-overexpressing cell line (A549, derived from a lung cancer patient) and incorporated cetuximab, a clinically validated benchmark antibody, to provide the EGFR-targeting component of the bispecific constructs.
The primary advantage of using cmLC antibodies in this context was the streamlined discovery process. Our single B-cell screening workflow concentrated solely on the heavy-chain variable domain, eliminating the need to maintain native LC-HC pairing, as all VH domains were inherently compatible with a single LC of known sequence.
In summary, our study demonstrates Clic and Flic as highly complementary antibody discovery platforms, each providing unique and synergistic contributions to sequence diversity, epitope diversity, and cross-species reactivity. The collective repertoires of Clic and Flic are impactful tools to generate next-generation NKp46 antibodies optimized for potent and tunable NK engagement.

Immunizations and single B cell screening
Immunizations of OmniClic animals with human NKp46 and recovery of B cells were performed as described for OmnidAb animals
34
. The OmniFlic animals were subcutaneously immunized with the same protein antigen in hock every 3–4 days for 6 weeks and B cells were recovered from lymph nodes instead of spleen. Single B cells were screened on the xPloration instrument, a microcapillary-based array screening system
33
using a bead-adsorbed protein target or a stable NKp46 CHO cell line (CHOK1-NKp46-Cell-Line, Kyinno Biotechnology, catalog number KC-1789). Hits were sequenced and unique-sequence clones were synthesized from custom-ordered DNA, expressed as full-length IgG1 and protein-A purified, prior to analytical characterization.
NGS processing
NGS data is preprocessed using pRESTO (0.7.1) from the Immcantation (Version 4.4.0) package and the resulting reliable antibody sequences from the preprocessing are annotated using IgBlast (1.18.0) that sources custom libraries for our OmniFlic- and OmniClic-derived antibodies. We then performed lineage analysis, clustering sequences with the same V and J gene, same heavy-chain CDR3 length, and an edit distance of two amino acids in the heavy-chain CDR3 region, to the annotated sequences from NGS libraries. When selecting clones, we first narrowed down to the lineages that contain both bead binders and cell binders from high throughput screening technique xPloration, reasoning that there is statistically high confidence in those lineages to bind with the target of interest. Clones are further selected using two methods. Method A selects clones based on the clone representation, picking the top and bottom 10 greatest representation clones from each overlap lineage. Method B selects clones that span across most lineages to capitalize on the diversity of the sequence space; the number of selected clones within each lineage is proportional to the size of the lineage. After selecting clones from both methods, we apply the liability assessment on both sequence and structural level to eliminate clones that have a high-risk developability issue.
Hit expansion
The data used for model building and selection included 69,000 unique heavy-chain amino acid sequences from NGS on three different OmniClic common light-chain chickens immunized with NKp46. Sequences were filtered for duplicate count greater than or equal to two. Activity data was provided for 178 unique amino acid sequences. Of the 178 sequences with activity data, 90 were inactive and the remaining 88 sequences had K
D
values ranging from 2 to 500 nM. Error values for the 88 active sequences were obtained by propagating uncertainty for association and dissociation kinetic rate constants (k
a
and k
d
) from the SPR measurements. K
D
values were scaled by -log2(K
D
) with inactive values set to zero corresponding to a K
D
2000 nM. This placed all the activity data for regression in the range of 0 to 10.
Variational autoencoder model
Antibody sequences were modeled using a VAE model
49
,
50
. Input sequences were embedded using 1-hot encoding into a 21 × 134 matrix where 21 corresponds to the 20 standard amino acids plus an end character and 134 is the maximum sequence length. Encoding was performed using an LSTM layer with 134 nodes and dropout regularization followed by batch normalization. The size of the latent layer was 50 nodes and was modeled using a multivariate normal distribution from tensorflow-probability with learned variances and covariances. The prior was a N(0,1) distribution and KL weight was 0.75. The decoder layer consists of an upsampling dense layer of size 67 × 36 followed by a 1D deconvolutional layer with 18 filters and kernel size and strides of 2 and ReLU activation, and an LSTM layer with 134 nodes. Each of the preceding 3 layers in the decoder is followed by batch normalization. A final dense layer of 21 nodes
50
forms the model output. A Gaussian progress regression model also comes off the latent layer. This model has one dense variational layer with trainable prior and 1 node with ReLU activation followed by a Gaussian Process regression layer. Dropout regularization is applied off of the latent layer input to the regression layer. Overall, the Encoder has ~260K trainable parameters, the decoder has ~210K trainable parameters and the regression model has 230 trainable parameters for a total of ~470K trainable parameters.
Model training
Model training was performed for 500 epochs using a batch size of 500 using an Adam optimizer with Nesterov momentum with a learning rate of 0.002. The autoencoder and Gaussian progress regression models were trained simultaneously in one global model. Loss weights of 1 and 50 were applied to the reconstruction loss and Gaussian process log-likelihood loss, respectively.
Clone selection
Sequences were selected from the VAE model using the Expected Improvement (EI) Bayesian Optimization acquisition function. All sequences with an EI value greater than an internal reference set by sequences with a measured affinity <25 nM. Sequences were filtered for liabilities at the structural level. In this case, six homology models were generated per sequence using the Molecular Operating Environment (MOE) software. Mean and standard deviation of the standard descriptors used in MOE were computed across all six models and these values were used for filtering the selection.
Surface plasmon resonance
Binding kinetics (capture kinetics) and epitope binning (classical sandwich) experiments were conducted using a high-throughput SPR (HT-SPR) on Carterra’s LSA platform equipped with HC30M as previously described
34
. Recombinant His-tagged human NKp46 protein was produced in-house (Uniprot Accession # O76036-1, residues 22 to 255) or sourced from Acro Biosystems (cat. no. NC1-H52H4) and recombinant His-tagged cyno NKp46 protein was sourced from Acro Biosystems (cat. no. NC1-C52H4). NKp46 proteins were polished by preparative size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) and monomeric fractions were isolated immediately prior to use. An anti-His mAb was used as a universal sandwiching control for all epitope binning experiments. Data were processed, analyzed, and figures generated using the Carterra EP™ software. Clones that performed as both ligand and analyte were amenable to a fully comprehensive bidirectional analysis, whereas clones that failed as ligand, were tested as analyte-only and therefore were not tested for mutual competition. To simulate a full heat map to facilitate hierarchical clustering into epitope communities, the blocking data from the 119 × 33 ‘many-on-few’ analyte-on-ligand heat map was used to infer ‘missing’ data (for analyte-only clones lacking a ligand counterpart) by transposing the measured blocking results (block or not block) and assuming a fully symmetrical pairwise competition matrix. The ‘inferred’ reconstructed heat map was then subjected to a user-defined cut-height to generate 14 epitope ‘communities’ (S3 Fig).
HDX-MS epitope mapping
Samples for HDX-MS analysis were named as follows: Sample-7 (F31), Sample-8 (F23), Sample-10 (C24), Sample-11 (C08), Sample-12 (C70), Sample-13 (C65), and Sample-15 (D01). Sample-7 to Sample-12 were analyzed in a separate experiment than Sample-13 and Sample-15. In-house-produced NKp46 was used for the HDX-MS experiments.
Sample preparation
HDX reactions comparing apo NKp46 to NKp46 incubated with Sample-7 to Sample-12 were carried out in a 10 µl reaction volume containing 30 pmol of NKp46 and 30 pmol of Sample-7 to Sample-12. The exchange reactions were initiated by the addition of 7.8 µL of D2O buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 92.6% D2O (V/V)) to 2.2 µL of protein (final D2O concentration of 72.3%). HDX reactions comparing apo NKp46 to NKp46 incubated with Sample-13 and Sample-15 were carried out in a 15 µl reaction volume containing 30 pmol of NKp46 and 30 pmol of Sample-13 or Sample-15. The exchange reactions were initiated by the addition of 11.8 µL of D2O buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 92.6% D2O (V/V)) to 3.2 µL of protein (final D2O concentration of 72.8%). Reactions proceeded for 10s, 100s, 1000s and 10000s at 20°C before being quenched with ice cold acidic quench buffer, resulting in a final concentration of 0.6 M guanidine HCl and 0.9% formic acid post quench. All conditions and timepoints were created and run in independent triplicate. Samples were flash frozen immediately after quenching and stored at −80°C until injected onto the ultra-performance liquid chromatography (UPLC) system for proteolytic cleavage, peptide separation, and injection onto a QTOF or Orbitrap for mass analysis, described below.
Protein digestion and MS/MS data collection
Protein samples were rapidly thawed and injected onto an integrated fluidics system containing a HDx-3 PAL liquid handling robot and climate-controlled (2°C) chromatography system (LEAP Technologies), a Waters Acquity UPLC I-Class Series System, as well an Orbitrap Exploris 120 Mass Spectrometer (ThermoFisher). The full details of the automated LC system were previously described
51
. The samples were run over an immobilized pepsin column (Affipro; AP-PC-001) at 200 µL/min for 4 minutes at 2°C. The resulting peptides were collected and desalted on a C18 trap column (Acquity UPLC BEH C18 1.7 µm column (2.1 × 5 mm); Waters 186,004,629). The trap was subsequently eluted in line with an ACQUITY 300Å, 1.7 μm particle, 100 × 2.1 mm BEH C18 UPLC column (Waters), using a gradient of 3–10% B (Buffer A 0.1% formic acid; Buffer B 100% acetonitrile) over 1.5 minutes, followed by a gradient of 10–25% B over 4.5 minutes, followed by a gradient of 25–35% B over 5 minutes, finally, after 1 minute, at 35% B a gradient of 35–80% B over 1 minute was used. MS experiments acquired over a mass range from 150 to 2200 m/z using an electrospray ionization source operated at a temperature of 200°C and a spray voltage of 4.5 kV. Same LC system, gradient and columns were used for all samples.
Peptide identification
Peptides were identified from the non-deuterated samples of NKp46 using data-dependent acquisition following tandem MS/MS experiments (precursor scan from 300 to 1500 m/z, 4 data dependent scans from 300 to 1500 m/z, dynamic exclusion set to
n
= 1 with 10s exclusion time, 6s expected LC peak width on Orbitrap system). MS/MS datasets were analyzed using FragPipe v18.0 and peptide identification was carried out by using a false discovery-based approach using a database of purified proteins and known contaminants
52–54
. MSFragger was utilized, and the precursor mass tolerance error was set to −20 to 20 ppm. The fragment mass tolerance was set at 20ppm. Protein digestion was set as nonspecific, searching between lengths of 4 and 50 aa, with a mass range of 400 to 5000 Da.
Mass analysis of peptide centroids and measurement of deuterium incorporation
HD-Examiner Software (Sierra Analytics) was used to automatically calculate the level of deuterium incorporation into each peptide. All peptides were manually inspected for, for example, correct charge state, correct retention time, and appropriate selection of isotopic distribution. Deuteration levels were calculated using the centroid of the experimental isotope clusters. Results are presented as relative levels of deuterium incorporation and the only control for back exchange was the level of deuterium present in the buffer (72.3% or 72.8%). Differences in exchange in a peptide were considered significant if they met all three of the following criteria: ≥5% change in exchange, ≥0.4 Da difference in exchange, and a
p
value <0.01 using a two-tailed student T-test. Samples were only compared within a single experiment and were never compared to experiments completed at a different time with a different final D2O level. The data analysis statistics for all HDX-MS experiments are in S3 Table according to published guidelines
55
(see S1 File for the source data file). The MS proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository
56
with the dataset identifier (PXD069455).
In-vitro developability assessment of anti-NKp46 antibodies
Thermal stability (Tm) and aggregation (Tagg) were determined by differential scanning fluorimetry (UNCLE-0330, Unchained Labs); and homogeneity and purity were assessed by analytical SEC as described previously
34
.
Generation of antibody models and in silico assessment of potential liabilities and post-translational modifications
For each of the eight clone sequences of interest (F15, F23, F31, C08, C24, C44, C65, C70), 25 Fv models were generated using Antibody modeler in MOE
57
. In all cases, a maximum of five different frameworks and five different CDR combinations of structural templates were used. All models generated were then subjected to energy minimization prior to structure-based annotation of potential post-translational modifications and liabilities. Liability score A, derived from previous work by Thorsteinson et al.
58
, was calculated for each model. It reflects the presence of exposed high-risk Asn deamidation and Asp isomerization motifs in the CDRs or framework, potential glycosylation sites within the CDRs, total CDR length, Fc total charge, VH-VL absolute charge difference, and size of CDR hydrophobic patch areas. We also used these models to evaluate potential unpaired cysteines in the CDRs and aggregation prone motifs (none to be reported), as well as to calculate the average isoelectric point (pI) and net charge at neutral pH
57
.
Production of bispecific antibodies for ADCC
Clones C08, C44, and F15 were selected for reformatting into a symmetrical tetravalent 2 + 2 scFv-IgG Morrison format using cetuximab scFv tethered from the C-terminal of the heavy chain (HC) or light chain (LC) of NKp46 Clic or Flic IgG backbone. Constructs were prepared in pairs: one construct had an active IgG1-Fc, the other incorporated STR silencing mutations
59
. Plasmids were constructed by following the manufacturer’s protocol of Gibson Assembly® Cloning Kit (NEB, E5510S) and amplified with EndoFree Plasmid Maxi Kit (Qiagen, 12,362). Proteins were expressed in HEK293 cells and protein-A purified followed by preparative SEC (Fig. S5c and S5d).
Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity assay
A 2D ADCC assay was performed by Charles River Laboratories, Inc. using the IncuCyte Live-Cell Analysis System for continuous visualization and automated analysis of immune cell-mediated killing of tumor cells (Sartorius, Inc). Donor-derived NK cells and EGFR-expressing target cells (A549) were used to test a panel of eight NKp46 X EGFR bispecific compounds, representing two Morrison formats. Six total donors were used, split into cohorts of three donors per Morrison format (to test four compounds per set of three donors) and each experimental condition was tested in triplicate. Each immune-assay readout was performed once. Readouts were tumor cell growth over time by IncuCyte.
The ADCC assay comprised 4 steps: target cell seeding, CD56-positive cells isolation, tumor killing assay, and data analysis, as follows. NucLight Red (NLR) expressing A549 cells were cultured under standard aseptic conditions. On day −1 these cells were seeded into Poly-L-Lysine coated 96-well plates at 7.5x10
3
cells/well. Human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from three healthy donors via density gradient separation. CD56+ NK cells were isolated from PBMCs by magnetic separation and CD56 purity was confirmed by flow cytometry prior to co-culture with target A549 tumor cells. Following CD56+ cell isolation, NK cells were incubated with target tumor cells expressing the NucLight Red (NLR) nuclear dye at a 10:1 effector:target (E:T) ratio. Co-cultures were incubated with 20 µg/mL bispecific compounds. Appropriate controls were included: tumor cells alone, tumor cells/NKs in the presence of 20 µg/ml Cetuximab (IgG1 targeting EGFR Control), 20 µg/ml IgG1 isotype control, 1 µM bortezomib (cytotoxic control) or 10 ng/ml IL-2+IL-12+IL-15 (NK activation positive control). Tumor cell growth was determined as the total red count (A549 NLR cells) per well normalized to
T
= 0. Area under curve (AUC) growth data was calculated in GraphPad Prism and reported as mean ± SEM (shown as error bars) of triplicate biological replicates. All samples were compared with untreated or vehicle (PBS alone): see S2 File for statistical T-tests.
